landing:
What you will make

Make an alarm with a Raspberry Pi Pico. You choose what it detects, how it warns and what it looks like.

Open the starter project and connect and test your Pico. Then pick any part:

  • Detect a change: choose a button, switch or sensor.
  • Give a warning: choose an LED, RGB LED or buzzer.
  • Decide with code: choose what sets it off and when it stops.
  • Bring it together: combine your chosen parts.
  • Make a case: choose your own shape and materials.
  • Test and Improve: try it, change something, try again.
  • Ideas to borrow: optional examples to spark your own idea.

Start with the parts you have. Each component page has wiring, code and a quick test. Mix your choices in any order after the Pico test.

options.title: Choose what counts as a trigger

1A.title: Connect and test your Pico
1A.html:
Connect and test your Pico

Everyone does this first. The starter checks the board before you choose any alarm parts.

Step 1

Try this

Download the starter project. Open it in Thonny and save your own copy as alarm.py.

Step 2

Try this

Connect your Pico with a USB data cable. In Thonny choose MicroPython (Raspberry Pi Pico) as the interpreter.

Step 3

Try this

Run your starter. Its first test is:

python
from picozero import pico_led
from time import sleep

pico_led.on()
sleep(1)
pico_led.off()
print("Pico and picozero are ready")

Test

Try this

Did the onboard LED light for one second? Did the Shell show Pico and picozero are ready? Keep your saved starter for the alarm you make.

Tip

If Thonny cannot find the Pico, check the USB data cable and interpreter. If it says No module named picozero, install picozero through Tools → Manage packages.

Choose a case, input, warning or rule next. You can change direction later.

3A.title: Button or homemade switch
3A.html:
Button or homemade switch

Detect when two contacts meet or separate. Use a push button, foil or another homemade switch.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug it before wiring.

Wire it

Try this

Gather a push button or foil and a card spacer.

Connect GP10 through the switch to GND. A four-leg button has joined pairs: follow the picture.

Try the code

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import Button

button = Button(10)

pressed = button.is_pressed

Add this to try a trigger. You can change the if line:

python
print(pressed)
if pressed:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Press and release, or join and separate your contacts. Run the code each time: can you get both True and False?

Make it yours

Should meeting or separating the contacts trigger your alarm? Use if pressed: or if not pressed:. You choose where the contacts go.

Ready? Connect it to your chosen warning.

3B.title: Touch sensor
3B.html:
Touch sensor

Detect a finger touching a pad with a TTP223 module.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug it before wiring.

Wire it

Try this

Gather a TTP223 touch module and three leads.

SIG goes to GP17, VCC to 3V3 OUT, and GND to GND.

Try the code

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import TouchSensor

touch = TouchSensor(17)

touched = touch.is_touched

Add this to try a trigger. You can change the if line:

python
print(touched)
if touched:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Touch and release the pad. Run the code each time: can you get both True and False?

Make it yours

Choose what touch does: trigger the warning, arm it or reset it. Bare foil contacts use the homemade switch circuit.

Ready? Connect it to your chosen warning.

3C.title: Toggle switch
3C.html:
Toggle switch

Detect which way a toggle switch is set.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug it before wiring.

Wire it

Try this

Gather an SPDT toggle switch and two leads.

Connect COM (centre leg) to GP6 and one outside leg to GND. Leave the other outside leg unconnected.

Try the code

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import Switch

mode = Switch(6)

mode_two = mode.is_closed

Add this to try a trigger. You can change the if line:

python
print(mode_two)
if mode_two:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Flip the switch each way and run again. Which position gives True?

Make it yours

Choose its job: trigger a warning, arm the alarm or select a mode.

Ready? Connect it to your chosen warning.

3D.title: Tilt switch
3D.html:
Tilt switch

Detect a change in angle. A small ball inside the switch makes or breaks a contact.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug it before wiring.

Wire it

Try this

Gather a ball tilt switch and two leads.

Connect GP8 through the switch to GND.

Try the code

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import Switch

tilt = Switch(8)

tilted = tilt.is_open

Add this to try a trigger. You can change the if line:

python
print(tilted)
if tilted:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Tip slowly and run again. Find the positions that give True and False; the reading may flicker while the ball rolls.

Make it yours

Choose an angle that should trigger your alarm. Use if tilted: or if not tilted: to match it.

Ready? Connect it to your chosen warning.

3E.title: Light sensor (LDR)
3E.html:
Light sensor (LDR)

Measure how light or dark it is with a light-dependent resistor (LDR).

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug it before wiring.

Wire it

Try this

Gather an LDR, a 10 kΩ resistor and leads.

Join the LDR and resistor at GP27. The LDR’s other leg goes to 3V3 OUT; the resistor’s other leg goes to GND.

Try the code

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import AnalogInputDevice

ldr = AnalogInputDevice(27)

light = ldr.value

Add this to try a trigger. You can change the if line:

python
print(light)
if light < 0.5:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Cover and uncover it, running the code each time. With this wiring, darker gives a lower value.

Make it yours

Choose light or darkness as your trigger. Change < to > for a higher reading, then choose a number between your two test readings.

Ready? Connect it to your chosen warning.

3F.title: Ultrasonic distance sensor
3F.html:
Ultrasonic distance sensor

Measure the distance to something in front of the sensor, without touching it.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug it before wiring.

Wire it

Try this

Gather a 3.3 V-compatible HC-SR04P ultrasonic sensor and four leads.

Trig goes to GP20, Echo to GP21, VCC to 3V3 OUT and GND to GND. Use the HC-SR04P, not a 5 V Echo module.

Try the code

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import DistanceSensor

sensor = DistanceSensor(
    echo=21, trigger=20
)

distance = sensor.distance

Add this to try a trigger. You can change the if line:

python
print(distance)
if distance is not None and distance < 0.3:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Move an object nearer and further away, running again each time. Readings are in metres; None means no echo.

Make it yours

Choose whether nearer or further away should trigger your alarm. Change 0.3 (30 cm) or <, keeping the is not None check.

Ready? Connect it to your chosen warning.

3G.title: Line sensor
3G.html:
Line sensor

Detect a change between a light and dark surface with a KY-033 sensor.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug it before wiring.

Wire it

Try this

Gather a KY-033 line sensor, contrasting card and three leads.

S goes to GP18, V+ to 3V3 OUT and G to GND.

Try the code

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import DigitalInputDevice

line = DigitalInputDevice(18, pull_up=False)

on_line = line.is_active

Add this to try a trigger. You can change the if line:

python
print(on_line)
if on_line:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Try a light and dark surface under the sensor, running again each time. Adjust its small dial until the reading changes.

Make it yours

Choose which surface should trigger your alarm. Try if on_line: or if not on_line:; you choose what moves past the sensor.

Ready? Connect it to your chosen warning.

3H.title: Potentiometer (dial)
3H.html:
Potentiometer (dial)

Turn a dial to give the Pico a reading between about 0 and 1.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug it before wiring.

Wire it

Try this

Gather a 10 kΩ potentiometer and three leads.

One end goes to GND, the middle to GP26, and the other end to 3V3 OUT. Check your dial’s leg order.

Try the code

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import Pot

pot = Pot(26)

setting = pot.value

Add this to try a trigger. You can change the if line:

python
print(setting)
if setting > 0.5:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Turn gently and run again at different positions. What are your lowest and highest readings?

Make it yours

Use the dial as a trigger, or let it adjust how sensitive another sensor is. You choose what the setting means.

Ready? Connect it to your chosen warning.

3I.title: Temperature sensor (TMP36)
3I.html:
Temperature sensor (TMP36)

Measure temperature in degrees Celsius with a TMP36 sensor.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug it before wiring.

Wire it

Try this

Gather a TMP36 sensor and three leads.

Flat face towards you: left to 3V3, centre to GP28, right to GND. Keep the legs apart.

Try the code

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import TemperatureSensor

convert = lambda voltage: (voltage - 0.5) * 100
sensor = TemperatureSensor(28, conversion=convert)

temperature = sensor.temp

Add this to try a trigger. You can change the if line:

python
print(temperature)
if temperature > 25:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Read the room temperature, then warm the sensor gently with your fingers and run again.

Make it yours

Choose warmer or cooler as your trigger. Set a temperature you can reach in your test and use > or <.

Ready? Connect it to your chosen warning.

3J.title: Temperature probe (DS18B20)
3J.html:
Temperature probe (DS18B20)

Measure temperature in degrees Celsius with a DS18B20 probe.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug it before wiring.

Wire it

Try this

Gather a sealed DS18B20 probe, a 4.7 kΩ resistor and leads.

VDD goes to 3V3, DQ to GP22, GND to GND. Put 4.7 kΩ between DQ and 3V3. Check your probe’s wire colours.

Try the code

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from machine import Pin
import onewire, ds18x20
from time import sleep_ms

bus = onewire.OneWire(Pin(22))
sensor = ds18x20.DS18X20(bus)
probes = sensor.scan()
assert probes, "Check probe wiring"
sensor.convert_temp()
sleep_ms(750)
temperature = sensor.read_temp(probes[0])
print(temperature)

Add this to try a trigger. You can change the if line:

python
if temperature > 25:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Run again to get a new reading. Only a sealed, waterproof tip goes in water; keep the Pico and connections dry.

Make it yours

Choose warmer or cooler as your trigger. Set your own temperature in the if line and allow time for the probe to change.

Ready? Connect it to your chosen warning.

4A.title: LED
4A.html:
LED

A single LED can give a bright, simple warning.

Before you test

Have you completed Connect and test your Pico? Unplug before wiring.

Wire it

Try this

Use an LED and a 220 Ω resistor. Connect GP11 → resistor → long LED leg and short leg → GND. The resistor must stay in the circuit.

Try the code

Try this

Try the Skills Bricks LED code:

python
from picozero import LED

led = LED(11)

led.on()

Add led.off() after looking at it. In your alarm, if triggered: can turn the LED on; else: can turn it off.

Test

Try this

Did it light? If not, check which leg is long, the resistor, GP11 and GND. Try placing it where a player can see it.

Choose when it warns on the bring it together page.

4B.title: RGB LED
4B.html:
RGB LED

Mix red, green and blue light. You choose the colours and what they mean.

Before you test

Have you completed Connect and test your Pico? Unplug before wiring. Use a common-cathode LED.

Wire it

Try this

Connect the R leg through 220 Ω to GP3, G through 220 Ω to GP4, B through 220 Ω to GP5, and the common long leg to GND. Each colour needs its own resistor.

Try the code

Try this

Try the Skills Bricks RGB LED code:

python
from picozero import RGBLED

light = RGBLED(red=3, green=4, blue=5)

light.color = (255, 0, 255)

Try light.color = (0, 255, 0) for green or (255, 0, 0) for red. Each number goes from 0 to 255. Use light.off() to switch it off.

Test

Try this

Can you make two colours that someone can tell apart? Put a label or shape beside the light so colour is not the only clue.

Choose when it warns on the bring it together page.

4C.title: Active buzzer
4C.html:
Active buzzer

An active buzzer has one built-in pitch. You can change its beep rhythm. Check the packet for active or built-in oscillator.

Before you test

Have you completed Connect and test your Pico? Use a small 3.3 V GPIO-compatible buzzer and unplug before wiring.

Wire it

Try this

Connect buzzer + → GP9 and − → GND.

Try the code

Try this

Try the Skills Bricks active-buzzer code:

python
from picozero import Buzzer

buzzer = Buzzer(9)

buzzer.on()
from time import sleep
sleep(0.25)
buzzer.off()

In an alarm, if triggered: can turn it on; else: can turn it off.

Test

Try this

Did you hear one steady pitch? Change the length, not its pitch, to make the warning yours. An active buzzer cannot play different notes.

Choose when it warns on the bring it together page.

4D.title: Passive buzzer
4D.html:
Passive buzzer

A passive buzzer can change pitch. Check the packet for passive or external drive; it can look like an active buzzer.

Before you test

Have you completed Connect and test your Pico? Use one small 3.3 V GPIO-compatible piezo buzzer on GP9 at a time.

Wire it

Try this

Connect buzzer + → GP9 and − → GND.

Try the code

Try this

Try the Skills Bricks passive-buzzer code:

python
from picozero import PWMBuzzer

# GP9, 2000 Hz, 50% duty
buzzer = PWMBuzzer(9, 2000, 32768)

buzzer.on()
from time import sleep
sleep(0.25)
buzzer.off()

Change 2000 to 1000 before running again to hear a different pitch.

Test

Try this

Did the pitch change? If not, check whether you have an active buzzer. You can make a new warning pattern.

Choose when it warns on the bring it together page.

5A.title: Choose what counts as a trigger
5A.html:
Choose what counts as a trigger

Choose the rule that sets off your alarm. You can start by inventing it, then try it with any input.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug before changing wires.

Choose a rule

  • Yes or no: a button is pressed, a pad is touched or a switch changes position.
  • Above or below: a distance, light level or temperature passes a number you choose.

Write it as “When ______, warn me.” Your component page has an if line to adapt.

Try an example: a light-level rule

Wire it

Use the light sensor circuit: LDR to 3V3, 10 kΩ resistor to GND, their join to GP27.

Try the code

This uses the Skills Bricks LDR setup. Run it in light and shade:

python
from picozero import AnalogInputDevice

ldr = AnalogInputDevice(27)
light = ldr.value
print(light)
if light < 0.5:
    print("Warn me!")

Change < to > for more light. Choose a number between your two readings.

Test

Try or act out both situations: one that should trigger your alarm and one that should not. Does your rule tell them apart?

5B.title: Arm and reset your alarm
5B.html:
Arm and reset your alarm

Arm means ready to detect. Reset means stop the warning. Choose how yours should work.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug before wiring; use a separate GP pin for each part.

Choose what happens

Your alarm could always be ready, or wait for a switch or touch. Its warning could stop when the trigger goes away, or wait for a reset action.

Try acting out the rule you want. You can design it before choosing components.

Try an example: an arm switch, button and LED

Wire it

Switch: COM to GP6, one outside leg to GND. Button: GP10 to GND. LED: GP11 through 220 Ω to its long leg, short leg to GND.

Try the code

Here, the switch arms the alarm. Releasing the button or disarming stops the warning.

python
from picozero import Switch, Button, LED
from time import sleep

arm = Switch(6)
trigger = Button(10)
warning = LED(11)

while True:
    if arm.is_closed and trigger.is_pressed:
        warning.on()
    else:
        warning.off()
    sleep(0.05)

Use your chosen input’s reading and warning action to change this rule.

Test

Try or act out your trigger and reset. If you have an arm control, what happens when the alarm is disarmed?

5C.title: Change the warning pattern
5C.html:
Change the warning pattern

Invent a flash or beep pattern. Start with the warning itself; you can add an input whenever you like.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug before wiring. Keep beeps short and comfortable.

Try a rhythm

Tap it out. Long or short? Fast or slow? Choose a pattern someone will notice.

Try an example: a flashing LED

Wire it

Use the Skills Bricks LED circuit: GP11 through a 220 Ω resistor to the long LED leg; short leg to GND.

Try the code

python
from picozero import LED
from time import sleep

warning = LED(11)
for flash in range(4):
    warning.on()
    sleep(0.2)
    warning.off()
    sleep(0.3)

Change the two times or the number of flashes. For beeps, use the setup and wiring for your active buzzer or passive buzzer instead.

Test

Try the pattern, or tap it to someone. Can they notice it? Once it is part of your alarm, check how quickly it stops when you reset it.

6A.title: Join one input and warning
6A.html:
Join one input and warning

Choose any input and any warning. Decide: when this happens, do that.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug before wiring. Give each signal its own GP pin; the circuits can share GND.

Combine your choices

  • Use the wiring diagrams for the parts you chose.
  • Put their imports and setup lines at the top of alarm.py.
  • Inside while True:, read your input and use its if line to start your warning. Use else: to stop it when the trigger goes away.

Keep taking a new reading inside the loop so your alarm can notice changes.

Try an example: a button and LED

Wire it

Button: GP10 to GND. LED: GP11 through a 220 Ω resistor to its long leg; short leg to GND.

Try the code

Add this below the starter test in your saved alarm.py:

python
from picozero import Button, LED
from time import sleep

button = Button(10)
led = LED(11)

while True:
    pressed = button.is_pressed
    if pressed:
        led.on()
    else:
        led.off()
    sleep(0.05)

For your own parts, use their setup, reading and warning commands. Keep the indentation and short pause.

Test

Try your rule, or act it out while you plan. What should start the warning? What should stop it? If a part does not respond, its component page has a small test to help.

6B.title: Add another input or warning
6B.html:
Add another input or warning

Give each part a job. Two inputs could trigger one warning, or one input could trigger lights and sound.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug before wiring. Give each signal its own GP pin; the circuits can share GND.

Choose a rule

Use or if either input should trigger the warning. Use and if both must happen. You can choose your parts and rule here, even if you have not built anything yet.

Try an example: two inputs, light and sound

Wire it

Button: GP10 to GND. Tilt switch: GP8 to GND. Active buzzer: + to GP9, − to GND. LED: GP11 through 220 Ω to its long leg, short leg to GND.

Try the code

Either input triggers both warnings:

python
from picozero import Button, Switch, LED, Buzzer
from time import sleep

button = Button(10)
tilt = Switch(8)
light = LED(11)
sound = Buzzer(9)

while True:
    if button.is_pressed or tilt.is_open:
        light.on()
        sound.on()
    else:
        light.off()
        sound.off()
    sleep(0.05)

Use your components’ setup, readings and actions in place of these. Change or to and to try a different rule.

Test

Try or act out each input alone, then together. Do the warnings match your rule? What should happen when neither input is triggered?

2A.title: Design your own case
2A.html:
Design your own case

What should your alarm look like? Sketch a shape, try materials or lay out your parts.

Before you test

Have you completed Connect and test your Pico? Do that before testing any circuit. You can sketch now and return.

Step 1

Try this

Choose a size and shape. Where will the sensor, warning and Pico fit? You can change your mind as you build.

Step 2

Try this

Try a quick shape or position. Leave room for the Pico, USB cable, input wires and warning light or buzzer. Keep the circuit removable while you test.

Test

Try this

Try the shape with your parts, or paper shapes the same size. Can the sensor reach what it detects and can someone notice the warning?

Choose any parts from Detect a change and Give a warning. Their pages have the wiring and code.

2B.title: Card and paper
2B.html:
Card and paper

Card and paper can hide the circuit or make the warning more visible.

Before you test

Have you completed Connect and test your Pico? Do that before testing the circuit. You can fold a model now.

Step 1

Try this

Fold a card case or stand. Mark where the input will sense a change and where someone can see or hear the warning.

Step 2

Try this

Leave an opening for the USB cable and a flap for fixing wires. If you use foil contacts, try where they meet and separate.

Test

Try this

Can you reach the Pico without tearing the case? Can the input still sense what it needs to sense?

You can change the shape once the circuit works.

2C.title: Reuse an object
2C.html:
Reuse an object

A box, bag, model or toy can become the alarm's home.

Before you test

Have you completed Connect and test your Pico? Do that before testing the circuit. You can choose an object now.

Step 1

Try this

Pick an object and decide what change it should notice. Try the movement before fixing any electronics to it.

Step 2

Try this

Support the Pico on removable card. Keep the USB socket accessible. Cover any loose metal that could touch the circuit by accident.

Test

Try this

Move or open the object. Can you put the input where it will detect that change reliably?

Use your chosen input’s diagram to plan where it will fit. Keep it easy to move while you experiment.

7A.title: Try it and improve it
7A.html:
Try it and improve it

Test whatever you have so far: an idea, a case, one component or a working alarm.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Stop the program and unplug before moving wires.

Choose a test

  • An idea: act it out. What should start and stop the warning?
  • A case: try the shape. Can the sensor and warning do their jobs?
  • A component: try its code. Does it respond the way you expect?
  • An alarm: try the trigger and reset. Does it also stay quiet when it should?

Change one thing

Try a different position, material, setting or rule. The component pages have wiring diagrams and code if you need help.

Test

Repeat your test. Keep the change if it helps, or try another idea. You can come back here whenever you like.

8A.title: Guard a model treasure
8A.html:
Guard a model treasure

Borrow this idea, change it, or ignore it. A model chest could warn when its lid opens.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug before wiring. Keep the 220 Ω resistor in the LED circuit.

Step 1

Try this

Put one foil contact on the lid and one on the box so they meet when shut. Treat them like the Skills Bricks button: one to GP10, one to GND. Add an LED and 220 Ω resistor on GP11.

Step 2

Try this

Start with this idea from the downloadable example:

python
from picozero import Button, LED
from time import sleep

lid = Button(10)
warning = LED(11)
while True:
    if not lid.is_pressed:  # foil contacts are apart
        warning.on()
    else:
        warning.off()
    sleep(0.05)

Test

Try this

Close the lid, then lift it. The LED should warn when contacts separate. If the contacts do not meet reliably, move them or add a small card flap. What else could a pair of contacts watch?

8B.title: Notice a visitor
8B.html:
Notice a visitor

Borrow this idea for a model shop, doorway or secret exhibit: warn when a hand gets close.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug before wiring. Use a 3.3 V-compatible HC-SR04P; do not connect a 5 V Echo pin to a Pico GPIO.

Step 1

Try this

Use the Skills Bricks circuits: sensor trigger GP20, echo GP21; RGB LED GP3/4/5 with one resistor per colour.

Step 2

Try this

This downloadable example uses green for ready and red when something is within 30 cm:

python
from picozero import DistanceSensor, RGBLED
from time import sleep

sensor = DistanceSensor(echo=21, trigger=20)
light = RGBLED(red=3, green=4, blue=5)
while True:
    distance = sensor.distance
    if distance is not None and distance < 0.3:
        light.color = (255, 0, 0)
    else:
        light.color = (0, 255, 0)
    sleep(0.1)

Test

Try this

Approach from different angles. Does 30 cm work for your design? Change 0.3 after checking what the sensor actually reads.

8C.title: Notice a moved object
8C.html:
Notice a moved object

Borrow this idea for a model artefact that complains when someone picks it up.

Before you test

Have you tested your Pico? Unplug before wiring. Use a small 3.3 V GPIO-compatible buzzer.

Step 1

Try this

Connect the tilt switch between GP8 and GND, and the active buzzer + to GP9 and − to GND.

Step 2

Try this

The downloadable example sounds while the switch is open:

python
from picozero import Switch, Buzzer
from time import sleep

tilt = Switch(8)
warning = Buzzer(9)
while True:
    if tilt.is_open:
        warning.on()
    else:
        warning.off()
    sleep(0.05)

Test

Try this

Move and replace the object. The switch can rattle, so find a position where it is settled when the object rests. Do you want the opposite angle to be the trigger?
